text: Multi-region strategy used to be one question: where should the app run to be close to users and survive a regional outage? AI infrastructure splits that into two different questions, because training and inference don't share the same constraints. Training is batch-shaped and nobody's waiting on it in real time, so it can run wherever it's practical. Inference is a live request a caller is blocked on, so every network hop adds latency they actually feel.

A training run's region should be chosen by GPU availability first — where the SKU you actually need exists — then by data gravity, since moving large training datasets repeatedly is slow and costly, then by cost once those two narrow the field. User proximity almost never makes this list. The people waiting on a trained model are waiting on when it finishes, not on network latency to the training cluster, so it's entirely reasonable to centralize training in one or two regions even for a model that will serve users worldwide.

Inference flips the priority order completely. What matters is where the users or calling services actually are, what the real latency budget is, and whether data residency forces serving into a particular region regardless of cost. A global routing layer — Front Door, Traffic Manager, Global Accelerator — then sends each caller to its nearest healthy regional deployment instead of one central endpoint everyone has to reach, which is what actually improves latency across a spread-out user base.

That multi-region inference footprint isn't free. Every additional region is additional GPU capacity to provision, scale, and pay for, which ties straight back to the cost discipline from the FinOps chapter. You replicate inference into a region because real users there genuinely need the latency, not by default, and not just because the architecture diagram looks more resilient with another box on it.

One thing can override both sets of reasoning at once: data residency. If a jurisdiction requires certain data, and the compute touching it, to stay within its borders, you end up running a smaller, separate training-and-inference stack for that region regardless of where GPU capacity is cheapest or where most of your users live. Next lesson turns to the SLOs that make 'is inference actually working' a measurable question instead of a feeling — latency, throughput, and availability as three distinct targets.
